scout.purpose: Metadata and language-shaped builders can make frameworks expressive, but they move behaviour away from ordinary direct calls and require disciplined boundaries.
scout.realWorldUse: Android build tools, Room, dependency injection, serialization, Compose, tests, and navigation use annotations, generated code, reflection, or Kotlin DSL patterns.
scout.outcome: Explain annotation processing and reflection costs, then design a small receiver-based builder whose scope remains unambiguous.

blocks.text: An annotation records metadata on a declaration, type, expression, or generated JVM element. @Target states where it may appear and @Retention controls whether it exists only in source, in compiled output, or at runtime. Frameworks can process annotations during compilation to generate code or inspect runtime annotations through reflection. Use-site targets such as field:, get:, or param: matter when one Kotlin property produces several JVM elements.

blocks.caption: The annotation carries a stable metadata value and is retained for runtime inspection.

sections.title: Prefer generated direct code when practical

blocks.text: Reflection inspects declarations or invokes behaviour dynamically. It reduces compile-time knowledge, may need extra metadata, complicates shrinking, and is harder to trace than a direct call. Compile-time generation preserves typed, inspectable code and often reports errors earlier. Room and many dependency-injection tools generate implementations from annotations. Reflection remains valid for tools and genuinely dynamic systems; isolate it behind a small adapter and cache repeated discovery instead of spreading reflective lookup through domain code.

blocks.code:
fun contentName(type: kotlin.reflect.KClass<*>): String? =
    type.annotations
        .filterIsInstance<ContentType>()
        .firstOrNull()
        ?.name

println(contentName(Expense::class))
blocks.caption: A small reflection boundary reads one known annotation and returns ordinary nullable data.

blocks.title: Metadata needs a consumer
blocks.text: An annotation alone changes nothing. Generated code, a compiler plugin, static analysis, or runtime logic must interpret it.

sections.title: DSLs use receivers to constrain vocabulary

blocks.text: A type-safe builder is usually a higher-order function with a receiver, such as ExpenseReportBuilder.() -> Unit. Inside the lambda, builder members can be called without repeating the receiver. The result should still be an ordinary validated model. DSL markers prevent accidental access to an outer receiver when builders nest. A DSL should make a repeated structure clearer; inventing language-like syntax for one simple constructor hides familiar Kotlin and raises the learning cost.

blocks.caption: The receiver supplies a limited vocabulary and build returns an ordinary read-only result.

blocks.text: Receiver scope deserves particular attention in nested builders. Without a DSL marker, an unqualified call may resolve to an outer receiver and modify the wrong object while still compiling. Mark related builder receivers, keep the vocabulary small, validate at build time, and return ordinary domain values so the special syntax remains confined to construction.

trap_check.mistake: Expecting an annotation to execute behaviour by itself.
trap_check.why: Metadata has no effect until a tool or runtime consumer interprets it.
trap_check.fix: Identify and document the annotation consumer and lifecycle.

trap_check.mistake: Creating a DSL for a single ordinary constructor.
trap_check.why: Novel syntax hides familiar code without reducing real repetition.
trap_check.fix: Use direct constructors until a repeated nested structure justifies a builder.

challenge_intro.task: Design a small receiver-based builder that validates expenses, prevents nested receiver confusion, and returns a read-only report.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: The DSL marker constrains nested receiver scope. Invalid expenses cannot enter the built report. The returned model does not expose builder mutation.

recall.prompt: What controls whether reflection can see an annotation?

recall.answer: It preserves compile-time checks, traceability, and often lower runtime overhead.

recall.prompt: What is the result of a good builder?
recall.answer: An ordinary validated model independent of the temporary DSL scope.

objectives: Describe annotation targets, retention, and consumers.
Contain reflection behind a focused dynamic boundary.
